name: Roman masonry arch
note: The wedge-shaped stone voussoir locked under compression. Rome perfected this; the arch remains the fundamental load-bearing form through the Middle Ages and beyond. Spans cannot be thrown long without collapse or immense depth, but the principle is unbreakable.

name: Barrel vault
note: An arch extruded in the third dimension: a continuous stone tunnel. Massive, permanent, and the ceiling form for the Basilica of Maxentius. Rome pushed vaults to extremes; Renaissance architects still marvelled at them.

name: Roman concrete dome
note: The Pantheon dome (126 AD) measures 43.3 metres and is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built. Pozzolanic concrete actually strengthens in seawater. Modern Portland cement does not; Pantheon beats it on durability.

name: Roman aqueduct with inverted siphons
note: Gravity-fed water under precise gradient over vast distances. At valleys, inverted siphons (pipes under pressure) carried water below ground, then up the other side. Rome's engineering was not obvious; this was clever and stable.

name: Roman paved road with surveying
note: Multilayered stone and gravel bed, crowned for drainage, aligned by groma (X-staff with plumb bobs). Roman roads lasted centuries. The technique is durable and maintainable; paving without surveying is wasteful.

name: Groma: Roman X-staff surveying tool
note: Four plumb bobs hanging from the four arms of a cross allow rapid sighting of right angles and straight lines. Crude and ingenious. Used to lay out Roman towns and roads across the empire.

name: Chorobates: Roman water levelling rod
note: A long wooden rod with a water-filled groove along its length: the water surface itself is a perfect level. Roman engineers used this to grade aqueducts with millimetre precision over kilometres. Needs no mercury, no instruments.

name: Roman sewer with gravity flow
note: The Cloaca Maxima in Rome still functions after 2400 years. Gravity-fed, arched, with gradient for scouring. Medieval towns often rebuilt sewers on Roman alignment; the Romans had solved the problem.

name: Roman fired brick and tile
note: Fired clay in standard sizes, facings for concrete, tiles for roofs. Uniform sizing was a Roman innovation; mass production of standard parts. The tiles lock together with ribs and survive centuries of weather.

name: Marble veneer and ashlar facing
note: Thin slabs of marble or stone cut to dimension and affixed to concrete, creating facade and surface. Aesthetic, durable, and separates structure (concrete) from facing, a principle unchanged to this day.

name: Insula: Roman apartment block
note: Multi-storey blocks of small rented rooms around a courtyard, using brick and timber joists. Rome housed its poor in dense urban clusters; the form remains standard. Fire risk was immense (hence frequent collapse in literature).

name: Glass panes for windows
note: By 100 AD Roman glassblowers produced clear soda-lime panes, often small. A luxury in Rome, it was still cheaper than oiled linen or mica. Roman houses with glass windows survive; the material itself is durable.

name: Amphitheatre with tiered seating
note: Concentric ovals of arched vaults and seating on filled earth. The Colosseum seated 50,000. Ruins of amphitheatres across the empire show that Romans mastered the geometry and structure of large public spaces long before the modern stadium.

name: Treadwheel crane
note: Large wooden drum turned by men inside a hamster wheel. Could lift tens of tonnes. Documented in Vitruvius; used to build the aqueducts and temples. Survives in medieval and Renaissance construction accounts.

name: Cofferdam and underwater concrete
note: Wooden piling in rings, the interior pumped or bailed dry, filled with pozzolanic concrete that sets underwater. Roman harbour piers used this. The concrete set faster in water than in air; not accident but observed principle.

name: Triangulated truss frame
note: A truss is fundamentally different from an arch: it carries load by rigid tension and compression in its members, not by geometric compression of wedges. A triangle cannot be deformed without changing member length. This is not intuitive; it requires understanding materials can pull apart.

name: King post roof truss
note: Two sloped rafters meeting at a peak, with a vertical king post from peak to tie-beam, and a horizontal tie keeping the rafters from thrusting outward. The tie is in tension, the post in compression. Simple and elegant; medieval roofs used this.

name: Queen post roof truss
note: Two vertical posts between tie and rafters, with a horizontal strut between them. Allows longer spans than king post without intermediate supports. The posts are in compression, the tie in tension, the struts shared the vertical load.

name: Timber trussed bridge
note: Timber trusses on stone piers. Spans to 80 metres were built. Timber is strong in tension and compression but rots; maintenance is perpetual. Covered bridges survive longer (dryness is the enemy of rot).

name: Cast iron bridge
note: Cast iron is brittle and strong in compression, weak in tension. Arched cast iron bridges (like the 1779 Ironbridge in Shropshire) mimic the arch form to keep the material in compression. Cast iron does not corrode like wrought iron but is prone to sudden brittle fracture.

name: Wrought iron working and riveting
note: Wrought iron from bloomery furnace is ductile, tough, and resistant to corrosion. Smith heating and hand-forging creates toughness. Rivets are driven hot; the cooled rivet locks parts together. Roman and medieval smiths knew this; it is not high art, but skilled work.

name: Wrought iron truss bridge
note: Wrought iron does not have the span of cast iron arches, but can carry tension. Wrought iron truss bridges (using the method of joints to proportion members) enable spans to 150 metres with light weight. Riveted wrought iron held up until the 1960s.

name: Drawn wire and wire rope
note: Fine wire drawn through successive dies, twisted into strands, twisted again into rope. Wire rope has the tensile strength of steel and flexibility of rope. Essential for suspension bridges. High quality drawplates are needed; brittle dies fail.

name: Suspension bridge with wire cables
note: Cables slung over towers and anchored at the ends, with vertical hangers supporting the deck. The cable takes the shape of a catenary under load (not a parabola). Long spans (1000m+) require understanding catenary geometry and high tensile wire. The first major suspension bridge was Brooklyn (1883).

name: Statics and equilibrium of forces
note: Force balance: sum of forces and moments at each point must be zero. Archimedes knew this; the formalism of vectors and moment arms is Renaissance work (Leonardo). Essential to size any structural member without collapse.

name: Method of joints for truss analysis
note: At each joint of a truss, forces are in equilibrium. By solving joint by joint (starting from known loads), the tension or compression in each member can be calculated. This displaced rule-of-thumb proportioning; calculation is faster and correct.

name: Bending moment and shear diagrams
note: A beam under load is bent. Shear forces and bending moments vary along its length; calculus (the derivative of shear is load, the derivative of moment is shear) gives the full distribution. Maximum moment indicates the critical section; this is what a designer must check.

name: Neutral axis in bending
note: When a beam bends, the top fibres go into compression, the bottom into tension, and there is a neutral surface in the middle with no stress. The stress magnitude increases linearly with distance from the neutral axis. This is why deep beams (I-beams) are efficient: material far from the axis is stronger.

name: Euler buckling of slender columns
note: A slender column under axial load will suddenly buckle sideways at a critical load, not from material failure but from geometric instability. Euler's formula shows the critical load depends on length squared and moment of inertia; long thin columns buckle easily. Calculation replaces guessing.

name: Theory of elasticity
note: Stress-strain relationship for materials. Young's modulus relates stress to strain; Poisson's ratio the transverse to axial strain. Allows prediction of deformation, not just failure. Requires testing to find material constants; without it, design is guesswork.

name: Factor of safety concept
note: Design load times a safety factor (typically 2 to 5) must not exceed the material strength. A codification of caution. Different factors for different risks; this is risk management, not ignorance. Without it, every overload is a surprise failure.

name: Materials testing and calibration
note: Pull samples to failure and measure the load. Cast a batch and test it; the material constants you need (tensile strength, Young's modulus, elongation to failure) come from experiment. No two batches are identical; testing catches the weakest.

name: Foundation piles and pile driving
note: Drive long timber posts into soft ground to reach firm strata. The pile takes vertical load and transfers it down. Rome used piles under the Theatre of Pompey; medieval builders drove thousands for cathedrals. Bearing capacity is guessed; soil testing came much later.

name: Spread footing on compacted soil
note: A wide stone or brick base distributes the wall load over a larger footprint. Soft clay will compress under load; settlement cracks the building. Soil testing (boring and observation) tells you what depth to go. Without it, you guess and hope.

name: Caisson and underwater excavation
note: A large hollow box sunk into water or soft ground, interior pumped dry, filled with concrete. London Bridge (1831) used caissons. Allows foundation work below water. Risk of leaking, and the deeper you go, the harder to keep dry.

name: Compressed air caisson and decompression
note: A steam-powered air compressor pressurises the interior, pushing water down. Men work under high pressure digging. Rapid decompression causes the bends (nitrogen bubbles in the blood). Slow decompression prevents it. Brooklyn Bridge (1883) lost 20 workers to decompression sickness; this is physiological, not mechanical.

name: Soil mechanics and bearing capacity
note: Terzaghi (1920s) developed the theory of effective stress and bearing capacity formulas. Before this, foundation depth was guess-work. Soil is not a simple material; water content, grain size, cementation all matter. Boring and sampling are the tools.

name: Rock drilling and tunnelling
note: Percussion drills (hitting, not rotation) cut rock slowly. Blasting with dynamite (nitroglycerin) broke larger rock faster (1867 onwards). Timbering the walls prevents collapse. Tunnels need gradient and drainage; straight-line surveying through a mountain is hard.

name: Tunnelling shield and incremental advance
note: A large cylindrical shield advances meter by meter through soft ground (clay, silt). Men dig at the face inside; segments are assembled behind; the shield is jacked forward. London Underground used this (1863 onwards). Prevents cave-ins but is slow and heavy.

name: Gravity dam in masonry or concrete
note: A thick wall holding back water by its own weight. Water pressure increases with depth (proportional to depth squared). The base must resist both the vertical load and the horizontal thrust. Most dam failures are not structural (cracking) but hydraulic (seepage, overtopping).

name: Arch dam in concrete
note: A curved dam transfers water pressure sideways to the canyon walls, not to the base. Thinner and lighter than a gravity dam. Requires rock walls on both sides and calculation of the arch stress. The Hoover Dam (1936) is an arch; it can hold a lake with less concrete than gravity.

name: Earth fill dam with compacted layers
note: Layered soil compacted by repeated passes. Far cheaper than masonry. Needs an impermeable core (clay) and stable slopes. Piping (internal erosion along a path of sand) is the enemy. Earth dams can be very large; Aswan High Dam is earth fill.

name: Spillway and flood management
note: A controlled overflow weir at a set height. If the dam fills above that level, water goes over the spillway, not over the dam. The spillway must carry high velocity water without erosion. Most dam failures are hydraulic: overtopping erodes the downstream slope.

name: Water treatment works and coagulation
note: Alum added to water causes clay particles to coagulate and settle. Sand filters then remove fine particles and some bacteria. Boiling kills most pathogens. Chlorine (post-1900) kills the rest. Water treatment makes urban life possible; sewage in the water kills you fast.

name: Pumping station and mechanical lift
note: A water-powered pump (or steam-powered later) lifts water uphill against gravity. The Archimedean screw predates Rome; centrifugal pumps came later. Lifting water to a tower gives pressure for distribution. Without lift, you must be lower than the source.

name: Water tower and pressure system
note: Water stored in an elevated tank. Pressure at the base is proportional to height (0.1 kg/cm2 per metre). Sufficient pressure to feed a city from a single tower. Replaces the Roman need for gentle gradients in aqueducts; now you can serve hilly ground.

name: Separate foul and storm sewers
note: Two pipes: foul (sewage) and storm (rain). Storm sewers are large but infrequent flow; foul sewers are constant. Combined sewers overflow during heavy rain, contaminating rivers. Separation is expensive but hygienic; Victorian engineers standardised it.

name: Sewage treatment works and activated sludge
note: Sewage (biological waste) requires aerobic decomposition. Activated sludge is bacteria and protozoa that eat organic matter when aerated. Germ theory explains why pathogens die in treatment; without it, the mechanism is invisible. Treated effluent is safe to discharge.

name: Steel frame building
note: A skeleton of steel beams and columns carries all loads; the exterior walls are non-load-bearing curtain walls. This is the essence of the skyscraper. Bulk steel (converter) and riveted or bolted connections. London's Great Exhibition building (1851) was a proto-steel frame; Chicago's Home Insurance building (1885) was the first true one.

name: Curtain wall (non-load-bearing facade)
note: Frames of iron or steel with glass or panels hung from the steel skeleton. The wall does not carry load; the frame does. Allows large glazed areas and flexibility. Every modern tall building uses this principle; it is inseparable from the steel frame.

name: Elevator with safety brake (Otis)
note: A steam-powered cab on a rope. If the rope breaks, mechanical wedges jam against the guide rails and lock the cab. Otis (1853) demonstrated this at a fair by cutting the rope; the cab held. Without the brake, nobody will ride it. The brake is the actual invention; vertical transport scales only after people trust their lives.

name: Reinforced concrete construction
note: Steel bars embedded in concrete take tension; concrete takes compression. Their thermal expansion coefficients happen to match (both expand at roughly 10-12 ppm/K). Steel does not rust in the alkaline environment of concrete. This works; Coignet patented it (1891). Allows thin slabs and long spans.

name: Prestressed concrete
note: Steel cables under high tension are embedded in concrete, then the tension is released. The concrete is compressed throughout. This pre-compression means the concrete can resist higher loads before cracking. Beams can span further. Freyssinet (1928) pioneered this.

name: Steel arch bridge
note: An arch of steel riveted or welded. Steel can be made into arched members with joints. Span to 500m. Requires calculation of arch stresses and support reactions. Sydney Harbour Bridge (1932) is a steel arch; it carries road, rail, and pedestrians.

name: Cantilever bridge
note: Pairs of cantilevers extend from towers toward each other, meeting or nearly meeting. Forth Bridge (1890) is a cantilever; it has massive rigidity. Requires deep towers and strong base connections. Spans to 400m. Rivals suspension in elegance.

name: Box girder beam
note: A hollow rectangular tube of steel or concrete. Material is placed far from the neutral axis (the walls), giving maximum rigidity with minimum weight. Bridges and long-span buildings use box girders. Torsional stiffness is also high; useful when spans are asymmetric.

name: Plate glass for windows and storefronts
note: Large flat panes of clear glass. Cast plate glass (poured onto a flat table, then ground and polished) allows sizes to 3-4 metres. Transforms storefronts and windows. Sheet glass (drawn from a bath) is cheaper but smaller. Large panes are fragile but stunning.

name: Fireproofing and fire-resistant structure
note: Steel loses strength at high temperature (500 C is critical). Concrete or ceramic encasement keeps the steel cool. Compartmentation (fire walls, fire doors) stops spread. The triangle: materials (incombustible), structure (load paths survive local fire), and exits (life safety). All three matter.

name: Building code and regulatory standards
note: Written rules for minimum structural capacity, fire safety, exits, materials. Enforced by inspection. The first comprehensive code was New York (1901). Codification stops guesswork and protects the public. Elite builders resist rules; lives saved prove the value.

name: Lightning conductor and grounding
note: A copper or iron rod running from the roof to ground rod(s) in moist earth. Captures lightning and shunts it safely into the ground. Franklin (1752) invented this; it saved many buildings. Reduces fire and injury. Requires good earth contact; a dry ground rod does nothing.

name: Theodolite for surveying angles
note: A telescope on a graduated circle; turns to measure angles to two objects. From a point, you can sight two distant landmarks and calculate their angle. Repeated sightings from multiple points give positions by triangulation. Accuracy to seconds of arc changes the scale of surveying from sight to hundreds of kilometres.

name: Precise levelling and level network
note: A telescope on a spirit level, with a graduated rod. From one point, sights the rod at a distant point and reads the height difference. Chain many such sightings and you have a network of height reference points. Modern mapping uses electronic total stations; the principle is 200 years old.

name: Town planning and street layout
note: Systematic design of streets, squares, and districts rather than organic growth. Rome's colonial towns used a grid (the orthogonal plan). Haussmann (Paris, 1850s) imposed radial avenues and parks. Planning is contentious (disrupts existing patterns), but saves lives (fire lanes, flood avoidance, sanitation) and improves efficiency.

name: Harbour and dock with breakwaters
note: A protected basin with stone or wooden walls. Breakwaters outside reduce waves. Quays allow cargo loading and unloading. Docks with gates can maintain constant water level despite tides. Venice was the model; modern container ports are different in scale only.

name: Canal pound lock for level changes
note: A chamber with gates at each end. A barge enters the lock, the gates close, water is let in or out (changing the barge's level), then the exit gates open. Brilliant: it allows a canal to climb hills without continuous flow. The canal network (1750-1850) moved goods and coal.

name: Sluice gate for water control
note: A wooden or iron gate that slides vertically in a groove, controlling the flow of water. Water pressure increases with depth (the force is immense at the base). The gate must be strong; friction resistance must be manageable. Used for mills, docks, and irrigation.

name: Dredging for channel maintenance
note: Sediment fills harbours and channels; dredges scoop it up. Early dredges were buckets on a chain driven by water power. Suction dredges (pump-driven) are later but far more powerful. Maintenance dredging is expensive and continuous. The removed material can be sold or used for land reclamation.

name: Paved street and sidewalk
note: Concrete or stone surface, crowned for drainage. Sidewalks segregate pedestrians from vehicles. Paving is expensive but lasts decades. Brick or stone is traditional; concrete (post-1900) is cheaper. Proper drainage prevents flooding and freezing damage.

name: Street lighting with electricity
note: Gas lamps (post-1800) were bright but hot. Arc lamps (post-1850) were bright and stable. Incandescent bulbs (post-1880) were safer. Electric grid power (post-1900) made street lighting universal. Crime dropped; nightlife boomed. The cost was perpetual maintenance of wiring and poles.
